Name: Frag_PrePaulineCreed
Title: The creed Paul says he received
ScholarlyNote: Recognised across the critical spectrum as a formula Paul inherited rather than composed: it uses vocabulary that is not his, it is structured for memorisation, and he introduces it with the technical language of handing on received tradition. Dating it to within a few years of the crucifixion is a majority position held by conservative and sceptical scholars alike, which is what makes it the strongest single link in the chain -- it is far too early for legendary development.

Name: Frag_PaulMeetsPeterAndJames
Title: Paul's first Jerusalem visit
ScholarlyNote: Paul places himself in direct contact with Peter and with James the Lord's brother within a few years of the events. Galatians is undisputed as to authorship, which makes this one of the few first-hand statements in the New Testament about who knew whom.

Name: Frag_PaulSeesRisenChrist
Title: Paul's own resurrection claim
ScholarlyNote: A first-person claim from a hostile party who changed sides. Its evidential weight is that Paul had every incentive not to make it; its limit is that he describes his own experience in terms that differ from the appearance accounts he cites just before it.

Name: Frag_WomenFirstAtTheTomb
Title: Women as the first witnesses at the tomb
ScholarlyNote: The criterion of embarrassment in its clearest form: in a legal and social setting where women's testimony carried little weight, no one inventing a story would choose women as the discovering witnesses. Note honestly that the four accounts differ on which women, how many, and in what order -- variation in peripheral detail alongside agreement on the core is what independent testimony to the same event actually looks like.

Name: Frag_PeterPreachingInRome
Title: Peter preaching in Rome
SourceReference: 1 Pet 5:13; Papias, via Eusebius, Hist. eccl. 3.39.15
ScholarlyNote: Contested because 1 Peter's authorship is disputed -- its polished Greek is hard to reconcile with a Galilean fisherman, though the letter itself names a secretary. The Roman location rests more securely on Papias and on 1 Clement than on the letter alone.

Name: Frag_MarkAsPetersInterpreter
Title: Mark as Peter's interpreter
ScholarlyNote: The load-bearing patristic claim for the whole Mark chain: Mark recorded Peter's preaching accurately but not in sequence. Papias is writing roughly two generations after the events and is himself preserved only through Eusebius, so the link is real but not short.

Name: Frag_GospelOfMarkComposed
Title: The Gospel of Mark as a written document
ScholarlyNote: The first complete narrative Gospel in Greek. Its own date is disputed within roughly AD 55-70 depending on whether Irenaeus or Clement is followed on its relation to Peter's death; see the campaign timeline row for the same event.

Name: Frag_PapiasOnMatthewLogia
Title: Matthew's sayings collection in the Hebrew dialect
ScholarlyNote: Contested on two fronts: what Papias meant by logia (sayings collection, or a full Gospel), and whether canonical Greek Matthew reads like a translation from a Semitic original -- most linguists judge that it does not. This is the pivot of the priority question, and the game's harmonisation treats the early Aramaic collection and the later Greek Gospel as two different documents.

Name: Frag_IrenaeusOnMarkAfterPeter
Title: Irenaeus on when Mark wrote
ScholarlyNote: Places Mark's writing after the departure of Peter and Paul, which is normally read as after their deaths and so after c. AD 64-67. Directly at odds with Clement on the timing.

Name: Frag_ClementOnMarkInPetersLifetime
Title: Clement on Mark writing in Peter's lifetime
SourceReference: Clement of Alexandria, via Eusebius, Hist. eccl. 6.14.6-7
ScholarlyNote: Places the composition during Peter's lifetime at the request of his Roman hearers. Cannot be reconciled with Irenaeus without straining one of them; the honest position is that the two earliest witnesses to Mark's date disagree, and the range AD 55-70 exists because of it.

Name: Frag_EusebiusOnPapiasJudgement
Title: Eusebius' low estimate of Papias
ScholarlyNote: The standard objection to leaning on Papias: the very writer who preserves him also judges him a man of small intelligence, on the basis of his millenarian views. A player building the Mark chain on Papias should expect to meet this in debate, and it is a fair hit -- Eusebius had the full text and we do not.

Name: Frag_IrenaeusOnPapias
Title: Irenaeus on Papias' standing
ScholarlyNote: Answers Eusebius' dismissal with an earlier and less hostile assessment: Irenaeus, writing some 140 years before Eusebius, describes Papias as a hearer of John and a companion of Polycarp. It does not settle Papias' judgement, but it establishes that a second-century writer with closer access rated his access to the tradition highly.

Name: Frag_IrenaeusFourfoldGospel
Title: The fourfold Gospel as settled
ScholarlyNote: By c. AD 180 the four-Gospel collection is treated as an established fact requiring theological justification rather than as a live question -- evidence that the fourfold shape was already settled well before Irenaeus wrote.

Name: Frag_ClementOnJohnSpiritualGospel
Title: Clement on John writing last
SourceReference: Clement of Alexandria, via Eusebius, Hist. eccl. 6.14.7
ScholarlyNote: Explains John's difference from the other three as deliberate: written last, supplementing rather than repeating. Useful because it shows the early Church noticed the divergence and accounted for it rather than papering over it.

Name: Frag_LukePrologueMethod
Title: Luke's statement of method
ScholarlyNote: A declared research methodology: prior accounts consulted, eyewitness sources investigated, an orderly account produced for a named recipient. It is a claim about method, not proof of it -- what corroborates it is the accuracy of Luke's incidental detail where it can be independently checked.

Name: Frag_ActsWePassages
Title: The 'we' passages in Acts
ScholarlyNote: Contested: the traditional reading takes the first-person plural as the author's own travel diary, placing him with Paul on the voyage to Rome. The main alternative treats it as a literary convention of sea-voyage narrative, though critics of that view note the convention is poorly attested elsewhere.

Name: Frag_ActsEndsAtHouseArrest
Title: Acts ends before the events that would date it later
ScholarlyNote: The central argument for dating Luke-Acts early: the narrative stops at Paul's house arrest without mentioning Nero's persecution, the deaths of Paul, Peter or James, or the destruction of the Temple -- all of which would have served the author's purposes. Contested because an argument from silence cuts both ways, and because many date Luke later on the basis of its apparent knowledge of Jerusalem's fall.

Name: Frag_JohnEyewitnessClaim
Title: The Fourth Gospel's eyewitness claim
ScholarlyNote: The Gospel asserts that its testimony comes from a named participant, but identifies him only as the disciple whom Jesus loved. Who that is, and whether the final form comes from him or from a community that preserved his testimony, is genuinely unresolved.

Name: Frag_1Clement5
Title: Clement of Rome on Peter and Paul
ScholarlyNote: Written from Rome within living memory of the events, referring to Peter's and Paul's sufferings as things his readers already know about. It is the earliest and steadiest evidence that both died at Rome; it does not describe the manner of death, and later accounts that do are considerably less secure.

Name: Frag_P52
Title: P52, the Rylands fragment of John
ScholarlyNote: Contested as to date. The early estimate of c. AD 125 rests on palaeographic comparison, and more recent work argues that such comparisons cannot support a range tighter than several decades -- placing it anywhere across the second century. The argument it supports is still real but weaker than it is usually made to sound: a copy of John circulating in Egypt well before the traditional sceptical dating of the Gospel.

Name: Frag_P66
Title: P66, Bodmer Papyrus II
SourceReference: Bodmer Papyrus II (P66), Gospel of John
ScholarlyNote: A near-complete copy of John from around AD 200, close enough in text to the fourth-century codices to show that the intervening century of copying did not substantially reshape the Gospel.

Name: Frag_P75
Title: P75, Bodmer Papyrus XIV-XV
SourceReference: Bodmer Papyrus XIV-XV (P75), Luke and John
ScholarlyNote: Its close agreement with Codex Vaticanus is one of the strongest single results in New Testament textual criticism: it showed that the Vaticanus text was not a fourth-century editorial creation but the faithful transmission of a much older exemplar.

Name: Frag_P46
Title: P46, the early Pauline collection
ScholarlyNote: Evidence that Paul's letters were circulating as a gathered collection, not as scattered correspondence, by around AD 200 at the latest.

Name: Frag_CodexVaticanus
Title: Codex Vaticanus
ScholarlyNote: One of the two great fourth-century codices, and with P75 the backbone of the modern critical text.

Name: Frag_CodexSinaiticus
Title: Codex Sinaiticus
ScholarlyNote: The earliest surviving complete New Testament. Its value to the argument is not that it is early in absolute terms but that it agrees so closely with the papyri two centuries older.

Name: Frag_LongerEndingAbsentInEarliestMSS
Title: The longer ending of Mark is absent from the earliest copies
ScholarlyNote: A real and unanswerable challenge, included because the design calls for textual variants to be faced rather than avoided. The two best fourth-century witnesses end Mark at 16:8, and the longer ending's vocabulary and style differ from the rest of the Gospel. Nothing in the evidence rebuts this. What can honestly be said is narrower: the passage is identified, its absence is documented in every modern edition, and no claim in the transmission chain depends on it.

Name: Frag_PericopeAdulteraeAbsent
Title: The pericope adulterae is absent from the earliest copies
SourceReference: P66; P75; Codex Sinaiticus; Codex Vaticanus (John 7:53-8:11 absent)
ScholarlyNote: The second variant the design insists on facing. The passage is missing from the earliest and best witnesses to John and appears at different places in later manuscripts, including in Luke. As with the longer ending of Mark, the honest response is not a rebuttal but a boundary: the text-critical process that identifies the intrusion is the same process that secures the rest.

Name: Frag_TacitusAnnals1544
Title: Tacitus on the Neronian persecution
ScholarlyNote: A Roman senator with open contempt for the movement records that its founder was executed under Pilate during Tiberius' reign, and that Christians were numerous enough in Rome by AD 64 to serve as scapegoats. The execution, the prefect, the reign and the spread are all confirmed by a source with no interest in helping.

Name: Frag_JosephusAnt20200
Title: Josephus on the death of James
ScholarlyNote: Widely accepted as authentic, unlike the longer passage in Book 18. A Jewish historian writing for a Roman audience identifies James by his relation to Jesus in passing, which is exactly the kind of incidental reference that is hard to explain as later Christian insertion.

Name: Frag_TestimoniumFlavianum
Title: The Testimonium Flavianum
ScholarlyNote: Contested, and the game should say so before a debate opponent does. As it stands in the received text the passage contains confessional statements no non-Christian Jew would write, and is certainly interpolated in part. The majority scholarly position is partial authenticity -- a shorter neutral notice that a later Christian copyist embellished -- with a minority holding the whole passage to be an insertion. Scored at a discount rather than discarded, which is what that majority position actually supports.

Name: Frag_PlinyEp1096
Title: Pliny's letter to Trajan
ScholarlyNote: A provincial governor asking the emperor how to prosecute Christians, describing their practice from interrogations. Establishes an organised movement in Bithynia by AD 112 that worshipped Christ as a god and would die rather than recant -- from an administrator investigating them as a public nuisance.

Name: Frag_SuetoniusClaudius25
Title: Suetonius on the expulsion from Rome
ScholarlyNote: Contested because the passage's key name is spelled in a way that may or may not refer to Christ, and Suetonius may have misunderstood his source. If it does refer to disturbances over Christian preaching in the Roman synagogues, it corroborates Acts 18:2 on the expulsion of Jews from Rome under Claudius.

Name: Frag_DelphiGallioInscription
Title: The Delphi inscription naming Gallio
ScholarlyNote: The anchor for the entire Pauline chronology. An imperial rescript fixes Gallio's proconsulship of Achaia to a narrow window around AD 51-52, and Acts places Paul before Gallio's tribunal in Corinth -- tying the narrative to a datable external record.

Name: Frag_PilateStone
Title: The Pilate stone
ScholarlyNote: A dedicatory inscription naming Pontius Pilate as prefect of Judaea, recovered at Caesarea in 1961. It confirms the office and title of the official under whom the execution is placed -- notably prefect rather than the procurator of later usage, which is the title the earliest sources use.

Name: Frag_ErastusInscription
Title: The Erastus inscription at Corinth
ScholarlyNote: Contested identification. A Corinthian pavement records an Erastus who paid for the paving in return for his aedileship, and Romans -- written from Corinth -- greets an Erastus who is the city treasurer. Whether the two are the same man turns on whether the Greek title Paul uses matches the Latin office, which is disputed.
